matrix.title: Be and Present Simple Foundations
matrix.summary: This lesson introduces two common ways to talk about the present.

keyTakeaways: Be for identity and state: am, is, and are describe people, places, and states.
Present simple for routines: the base verb describes habits and facts.
Negative forms: not follows be; do not supports a main verb.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Present Simple vs Present Continuous
matrix.summary: Both tenses describe the present, but they show different ways of viewing an event.

keyTakeaways: Present simple presents routines, repeated events, timetables, and facts.
Present continuous presents actions in progress and temporary situations.
Choose by intended meaning, not by one signal word alone.
reviewPrompts: Describe one normal routine and one temporary change this week.
Explain the difference between 'I live here' and 'I am living here for now.'

matrix.title: Present Perfect vs Past Simple
matrix.summary: The central contrast is not 'recent versus old'; it is finished past time versus a past-to-present connection.

keyTakeaways: Past simple anchors an event to finished past time.
Present perfect connects past and present or uses an unfinished time frame.
A finished time expression normally blocks the present perfect.
reviewPrompts: Write one life-experience sentence, then add a finished date using the past simple.
Explain why 'I have called her yesterday' is not standard.

matrix.title: Past Perfect and Future Perfect Forms
matrix.summary: Use perfect and continuous aspect to position events precisely in past narratives and future plans.

keyTakeaways: Earlier past: Use past perfect for an event completed before another past reference point.
Future in progress: Use future continuous for an activity that will be happening at a particular future time.
Future completed result: Use future perfect for something completed before a stated future deadline or point.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Tense Choice for Nuance and Discourse
matrix.summary: Select tense and aspect to manage narrative viewpoint, discourse framing, and the relationship between events.

keyTakeaways: Narrative viewpoint: Use past simple for the main sequence and past perfect for a prior background event.
Current relevance: Use present perfect for a past event linked to now; use past simple with a finished time reference.
Marked present: A present form can make a narrative vivid or state a general interpretation of past evidence.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Can for Ability, Permission, and Requests
matrix.summary: Can is a flexible beginner modal for what is possible, possible to do, or allowed.

keyTakeaways: Can plus base verb: can is followed by the base verb.
Cannot and can't: the negative form says that something is not possible or allowed.
Can I...?: a question can ask for permission or help.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Modals A2: Advice and Obligation
matrix.summary: Use should, must, and have to to manage advice, rules, and everyday obligations.

keyTakeaways: Advice with should: Use should + base verb when you recommend an action without making it a rule.
Strong obligation: Must often expresses the speaker’s strong rule; have to often points to an outside requirement.
Two different negatives: Mustn’t means prohibited; don’t have to means optional or unnecessary.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Might, Could, and Basic Deduction
matrix.summary: Use modal verbs to express possibility and make careful deductions about present situations.

keyTakeaways: Possibility: Use might or could when an event is possible but not certain.
Strong deduction: Use must when the available evidence makes a conclusion very likely.
Negative deduction: Use can’t when the evidence makes a conclusion impossible or very unlikely.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Perfect Modals for Past Judgement
matrix.summary: Use perfect modal forms to assess past possibility, obligation, regret, and alternative outcomes.

keyTakeaways: Past deduction: Use a perfect modal to assess what probably, possibly, or impossibly happened.
Past expectation: Should have often expresses criticism or an action that would have been better.
Unrealised option: Could have describes an option that was available but was not taken.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Nuanced Modality and Hedging
matrix.summary: Use modal expressions to calibrate certainty, obligation, politeness, and academic or professional stance.

keyTakeaways: Epistemic hedging: These forms signal possibility or a cautious interpretation rather than certainty.
Calibrated expectation: Choose the expression according to whether the expectation is normative, advisory, or evidence-based.
Stance and distance: These phrases let a writer state a considered view while leaving room for qualification.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Passive A1 pathway
matrix.summary: Planned A1 progression for passive.

matrix.title: Present Passive for Simple Processes
matrix.summary: Describe products, signs, and repeated processes with the present passive.

keyTakeaways: Be plus past participle: The present passive uses a form of be and the past participle: is made, are checked.
Singular and plural agreement: Choose is or are from the affected noun, not from the hidden doer.
Process focus: Use passive wording when the process, product, or result is the useful information.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Passive Forms Across Common Tenses
matrix.summary: Use passive forms across present, past, perfect, and modal contexts when the affected thing matters.

keyTakeaways: Tense stays visible: Change the form of be to show tense: is repaired, was repaired, has been repaired.
Modal passive: After a modal, use be + past participle: The form must be signed.
Focus and agent: Add a by phrase only when the agent adds useful information.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Passive Voice Across Tenses and Modals
matrix.summary: Use passive voice flexibly in reports, policies, and explanations across complex tense and modal contexts.

keyTakeaways: Perfect passive: Perfect passive forms show an affected result completed before a reference point.
Modal passive: Use modal passive for requirements or deductions about an affected event.
Agent and focus: Include the agent when accountability, authorship, or source is relevant.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Impersonal and Sophisticated Passive
matrix.summary: Use passive reporting and causative structures to foreground evidence, processes, and institutional stance.

keyTakeaways: Impersonal reporting: Use an impersonal passive to present a claim as part of an evidence or discourse field.
Subject raising: Structures such as is thought to have reflect a reported conclusion about the subject.
Causative passive: Use have or get something done when a subject arranges for another person or process to do it.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic If and When Conditions
matrix.summary: An if-clause makes a small cause-and-result connection.

keyTakeaways: If introduces a condition: if says what must happen first.
Present form for familiar results: both clauses can use the present simple.
Comma and clause order: a fronted if-clause is followed by a comma.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Real Conditions and Likely Results
matrix.summary: Connect a possible condition with a likely result or practical plan.

keyTakeaways: If plus present: Use present simple after if even when the meaning is about the future.
Likely result: Use will in the result clause for a likely consequence, promise, or plan.
Unless: Unless introduces the condition that something does not happen.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Zero, First, and Second Conditionals
matrix.summary: Conditionals connect a condition with its result. The form shows how the speaker views that relationship.

keyTakeaways: Zero = general relationship.
First = realistic future possibility.
Second = imagined or remote present/future situation.
The past form in the second conditional marks distance, not past time.
reviewPrompts: Describe one general result, one real plan, and one imagined change.
Change a first conditional into a second conditional and explain the viewpoint shift.

matrix.title: Third Conditional and Unfulfilled Past Conditions
matrix.summary: Use the third conditional to discuss unreal past conditions and their imagined consequences.

keyTakeaways: Unreal past condition: Use had + past participle for a condition that did not happen in the past.
Imagined past result: Choose the modal according to certainty, ability, or possibility of the imagined result.
Mixed consequence: A past condition can explain a present situation when the consequence continues now.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Mixed Conditionals and Inversion
matrix.summary: Use mixed conditionals and inverted conditional clauses to connect hypothetical causes, consequences, and formal register.

keyTakeaways: Past cause, present result: Use this mixed form when an unreal past event explains a present situation.
Conditional inversion: Omit if in formal conditions by placing had, were, or should before the subject.
Register and reality: Choose the result modal to show consequence, possibility, or tentative evaluation.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Subject–Verb–Object Order
matrix.summary: English basic sentences are easiest to understand when the actor comes before the action.

keyTakeaways: Subject before verb: the subject shows who or what acts.
Object after the verb: the object receives the action.
Place and time phrases: short place or time phrases often follow the object.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Adverb Placement in Everyday Sentences
matrix.summary: Place frequency, manner, time, and place adverbs clearly in everyday sentences.

keyTakeaways: Frequency with be: Frequency adverbs usually follow be: She is often early.
Frequency with a main verb: Put common frequency adverbs before an ordinary main verb: They usually walk.
Manner and time: Manner often follows the object; time and place can come later or move to the front.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Word Order in Complex Sentences
matrix.summary: Keep complex sentences clear by placing clauses, adverbs, and information focus where readers expect them.

keyTakeaways: Clause adjacency: Place an adverb or subordinate clause close to the verb or idea it describes.
Adverb position: Adverbs such as already, still, and probably usually sit near the auxiliary or main verb.
Fronted information: A fronted time, condition, or contrast phrase can guide the reader before the main point.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Emphatic Word Order and Information Focus
matrix.summary: Reshape sentence order to highlight contrast, correction, or the most important information.

keyTakeaways: It-cleft focus: Use an it-cleft to identify the element that deserves emphasis.
What-cleft focus: A what-cleft presents an action or idea first and its important result second.
Marked inversion: Fronted limiting expressions can trigger auxiliary inversion in formal emphasis.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Emphasis with Clefts, Inversion, and Auxiliaries
matrix.summary: Advanced emphasis changes information structure: it tells the reader or listener what to notice most strongly.

keyTakeaways: Clefts isolate the information in focus.
Fronted negative or restrictive adverbials trigger auxiliary–subject inversion.
Emphatic do/does/did strengthens a correction or contrast.
Advanced emphasis is a discourse and register choice, not decoration.
reviewPrompts: Express the same focus once with an it-cleft and once with a wh-cleft.
Find one ordinary sentence in formal writing and rewrite it with appropriate inversion.

matrix.title: Basic Yes/No and Wh- Questions
matrix.summary: Questions open a conversation by asking for confirmation or one missing detail.

keyTakeaways: Be questions: be comes before the subject.
Do and does questions: do/does supports a present-simple main verb.
Wh- words: the wh-word asks for a specific detail.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Past and Future Questions
matrix.summary: Ask clear questions about finished events and future plans.

keyTakeaways: Past action questions: Did carries the past question, so the main verb stays in its base form.
Future questions: Use will for a decision or expectation and be going to for a plan.
Questions with be: When be is the main verb, move was or were before the subject.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Indirect Questions
matrix.summary: Ask for information politely and embed questions inside longer clauses.

keyTakeaways: Yes/no embedding: Use if or whether and do not invert the subject and verb after the opening phrase.
Wh embedding: Keep the wh-word but use normal statement order: Do you know where she lives?
Polite openings: These openings make a request for information less direct.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Embedded and Complex Questions
matrix.summary: Build complex questions that combine polite framing, alternatives, and multiple layers of information.

keyTakeaways: Formal embedding: A formal opening is followed by a clause with statement word order.
Alternatives: Use whether ... or to ask which of two possibilities is true.
Question about a subject: When the question word is the subject, do not add do or invert the verb.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Rhetorical and Nuanced Questions
matrix.summary: Use question forms to challenge assumptions, manage disagreement, and invite reflection without always seeking factual information.

keyTakeaways: Rhetorical framing: A rhetorical question can introduce an issue without requiring a literal answer.
Negative expectation: A negative question can signal that the speaker expected agreement or confirmation.
Clarifying distance: A carefully framed question can request precision without sounding openly confrontational.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Negation with Not, Don’t, and Doesn’t
matrix.summary: Negation lets a speaker say that a state, place, or routine is not true.

keyTakeaways: Not after be: be + not makes a negative state.
Do not and does not: do-support carries present-simple negation.
Base verb after does not: does not already carries the third-person ending.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Never, Nothing, and Stronger Negation
matrix.summary: Use negative adverbs and pronouns without creating double negatives.

keyTakeaways: Never for frequency: Never means at no time and normally comes before an ordinary main verb.
Negative pronouns: Nothing means no thing, nobody no person, and nowhere no place.
One negative idea: Use one clear negative structure rather than two negatives together.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Negative Constructions for Nuance
matrix.summary: Use negative adverbs and patterns to express limits, frequency, and change precisely.

keyTakeaways: Low degree: Hardly means almost not or almost never and is weaker than an absolute negative.
Rare frequency: Rarely and seldom mean not often and are more formal than not often.
Changed situation: No longer means that something was true before but is not true now.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Prefixes and Complex Negation
matrix.summary: Form precise negative meanings with prefixes and multiword negative constructions.

keyTakeaways: Negative prefixes: Prefixes create a negative, opposite, or incorrect meaning, but the correct prefix depends on the word.
Negative scope: These expressions limit or reject a conclusion without making an absolute negative claim.
Formal emphasis: A strong fronted negative expression can require auxiliary inversion in formal writing.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Negative Inversion and Scope
matrix.summary: Use negative and limiting expressions with inversion to create formal emphasis and control the scope of a claim.

keyTakeaways: Negative inversion: Fronted negative adverbs trigger inversion in formal or emphatic writing.
Limiting inversion: Only expressions can foreground a condition or time and invert the following clause.
Scope control: These patterns limit or redirect the negative meaning precisely.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Dependent Clauses with Because, When, and If
matrix.summary: Clauses let a learner connect simple ideas instead of writing every idea as a separate sentence.

keyTakeaways: Main and dependent clause: a main clause can stand alone; a dependent clause needs a main idea.
Because for reason: because explains why.
When and if: when gives time; if gives a condition.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Because, When, and If Clauses
matrix.summary: Join a main clause to a reason, time, or condition.

keyTakeaways: Reason with because: Because introduces the reason for an action or situation.
Time with when: When connects two events by showing when one happens.
Condition with if: If introduces a possible condition; add a comma when the if-clause comes first.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Subordinate Clauses for Contrast and Time
matrix.summary: Combine ideas with subordinate clauses that show contrast, time, and condition.

keyTakeaways: Contrast: Although and even though introduce a contrast that does not stop the main result.
Comparison in clauses: While and whereas can place two situations side by side for contrast.
Condition and time: Unless introduces an if-not condition; as soon as links an immediate result to a future event.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Complex Clause Combinations
matrix.summary: Combine coordination and subordination to express layered relationships between ideas.

keyTakeaways: Layered relationships: Use different linkers to show which relationship is primary and which is additional.
Concession with despite: Despite is followed by a noun phrase or gerund unless it includes the fact that.
Scope and punctuation: Use commas and clause order to make the scope of a condition or contrast clear.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Reduced and Embedded Clauses
matrix.summary: Use reduced, nominal, and embedded clauses to package complex propositions concisely.

keyTakeaways: Reduced circumstance: Reduce a subordinate clause when the subject is shared and the relationship remains clear.
Nominal embedding: Package a full proposition as a noun phrase for reference in a larger sentence.
Non-finite purpose/result: Use non-finite clauses to compress purpose or an unexpected result.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Article Reference: a, an, and the
matrix.summary: Articles help a listener know whether a noun is new, identifiable, or general.

keyTakeaways: A and an introduce one: a/an introduces one countable noun.
The identifies: the points to a known or specific noun.
General uncountable reference: some general substances and activities can have no article.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Common Article Choices
matrix.summary: Choose a, an, the, or no article for new, known, general, and unique things.

keyTakeaways: First mention: Use a or an when you mention one non-specific countable thing for the first time.
Known or unique reference: Use the when both people know which thing you mean or it is unique in context.
General ideas: Use no article for general plural ideas and many general uncountable ideas.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Zero Article and Specific Reference
matrix.summary: Choose articles for institutions, meals, transport, and general concepts when context changes the meaning.

keyTakeaways: Institutional function: Some institutions take zero article when the person is there for the usual function.
Specific reference: Use the when referring to a particular building, object, or occasion rather than its general function.
General concepts: General ideas such as education, patience, and books often take no article.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Articles with Abstract and General Reference
matrix.summary: Use articles to distinguish broad concepts, established institutions, and specific abstract references in formal English.

keyTakeaways: Broad abstraction: Use no article when discussing an abstract concept in general: Research takes time.
Defined system: Use the when the concept is limited by a phrase or understood as a particular system.
General plural reference: Plural nouns can refer to a class or category in general without an article.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Stylistic and Idiomatic Article Use
matrix.summary: Use articles flexibly in idioms, institutional language, generalisations, and stylistic contrasts.

keyTakeaways: Idiomatic reference: Some fixed expressions require an article regardless of broad meaning.
Institutional contrast: Zero article can signal institutional function; the can identify a particular place or organisation.
Category reference: Use the to refer collectively to a social category or a representative class.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Singular, Plural, and Basic Quantity
matrix.summary: Countability changes the noun form and the quantity word that can go with it.

keyTakeaways: Countable nouns: countable nouns can have one or more forms.
Some and any: some is common in positive clauses; any is common in questions and negatives.
Much and many: many counts items; much measures an uncountable amount.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Much, Many, and Everyday Quantities
matrix.summary: Match quantity words to countable and uncountable nouns.

keyTakeaways: Many with countable nouns: Use many when the noun refers to separate items or people.
Much with uncountable nouns: Use much with uncountable amounts, especially in questions and negatives.
A lot of in affirmation: A lot of is natural for large amounts and numbers in everyday affirmative sentences.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Tricky Uncountable Nouns
matrix.summary: Treat common uncountable nouns accurately and add a unit when you need to count them.

keyTakeaways: Uncountable vocabulary: These nouns describe substance, knowledge, or a collection and normally do not take plural -s.
Units: Use a unit expression when counting one part or example of an uncountable noun.
Meaning changes: Some nouns change countability when they mean an event, document, or physical object.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Abstract Nouns and Count Shifts
matrix.summary: Recognise when abstract nouns change from uncountable concepts to countable events, types, or items.

keyTakeaways: Concept meaning: Use the uncountable meaning for a general activity, knowledge, trade, or illumination.
Instance meaning: Use the countable meaning for separate events, companies, lamps, or types.
Meaning plus determiner: The determiner helps signal whether the noun means a substance/concept or a separate instance.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Nuanced Countability and Mass Reference
matrix.summary: Choose countable and uncountable readings to express types, substances, practices, and abstract fields precisely.

keyTakeaways: Field versus instance: The uncountable form describes a field or accumulated knowledge; the plural form describes separate studies or events.
Type and variety: Use type expressions when comparing varieties of an otherwise mass or abstract noun.
Agreement and scope: Verb agreement follows the reading intended in the sentence.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: This, That, These, Those, and Some
matrix.summary: Determiners point to a noun or show how much of it is meant.

keyTakeaways: This and that: this is near; that is farther away.
These and those: these and those are plural forms.
Some for an open set: some avoids naming an exact amount.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Any, Many, Few, and A Few
matrix.summary: Use common quantity determiners for questions, negatives, and small numbers.

keyTakeaways: Any in questions and negatives: Any asks whether even one exists and is common in negative statements.
Many with plural nouns: Many describes a large number of separate items or people.
Few and a few: The article changes the speaker’s attitude toward the small number.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Either, Neither, and Both
matrix.summary: Use paired determiners to talk about two alternatives, two negative options, or two shared facts.

keyTakeaways: Both: Both includes the two people or things in the statement.
Either: Either selects one of two alternatives, usually in a choice or condition.
Neither: Neither rejects both alternatives and normally takes a singular noun or verb in formal writing.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Complex Quantification
matrix.summary: Use quantifiers and distributive determiners precisely when referring to groups, amounts, and alternatives.

keyTakeaways: Group and distribution: All views a group together; each and every distribute attention across members.
Number and amount: Choose number for countable items and amount for substances or abstract quantities.
Alternative quantity: Match the determiner and verb to the alternatives being discussed.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Subtle Reference and Quantification
matrix.summary: Use advanced determiners to distinguish totality, distribution, approximation, and open-ended reference.

keyTakeaways: Distribution and totality: Each distributes attention to members; every generalises across members; all views the group collectively.
Open choice: These forms leave the choice open while preserving the condition or result.
Scope and exception: Use any for unrestricted choice or emphasis and all but to state an exception.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Personal and Possessive Pronouns
matrix.summary: Pronouns keep a sentence from repeating the same noun.

keyTakeaways: Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, and they do the action.
Object pronouns: me, you, him, her, it, us, and them receive an action.
Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, its, our, and their come before a noun.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Object and Possessive Pronouns
matrix.summary: Use object pronouns after verbs and possessive pronouns without repeating nouns.

keyTakeaways: Object forms: Use object pronouns after a verb or preposition.
Possessive pronouns: Use a possessive pronoun when the noun is already understood.
Determiner versus pronoun: A possessive determiner comes before a noun; a possessive pronoun stands alone.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Reflexive and Indefinite Pronouns
matrix.summary: Use reflexive and indefinite pronouns to identify the actor, shared action, or an unknown person or thing.

keyTakeaways: Reflexive action: Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object refer to the same person.
Shared action: Use each other when two or more people do the action mutually.
Indefinite reference: Choose the indefinite pronoun according to affirmative, question, or negative meaning.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Reference Across Complex Text
matrix.summary: Maintain clear reference with this, that, which, one, ones, and they across connected sentences.

keyTakeaways: Idea reference: This and that can refer to a previous statement, with distance or evaluation depending on context.
Substitution: Use one or ones to avoid repeating a countable noun after a determiner or adjective.
Clear antecedent: Choose a pronoun only when the reader can identify its antecedent without guessing.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Sophisticated Cohesion and Reference
matrix.summary: Use pronouns and substitution devices to maintain cohesion across paragraphs without ambiguity or repetition.

keyTakeaways: Whole-clause reference: A pronoun can refer to an entire preceding proposition rather than one noun.
Substitution: Use substitution to avoid repeating a noun or verb phrase when the reference is clear.
Cataphoric reference: A pronoun can anticipate a later explanation, especially in formal framing.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Verb-ing after Like, Love, and Enjoy
matrix.summary: A gerund lets a beginner talk about an activity as a thing.

keyTakeaways: Verb-ing as an activity: an -ing form can name an activity.
Like, love, and enjoy: common preference verbs can be followed by verb-ing.
Negative preference: do not or does not carries the negative.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Common Verb + Gerund Patterns
matrix.summary: Use -ing after common verbs, prepositions, and leisure expressions.

keyTakeaways: Verb plus gerund: These common verbs are followed by an activity in -ing form.
Preposition plus gerund: A preposition is followed by the activity form, not an infinitive.
Go plus activity: Use go + -ing for many leisure activities such as cycling and shopping.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Verb Patterns with Gerunds
matrix.summary: Use gerunds after a wider range of verbs and distinguish activity patterns that change meaning.

keyTakeaways: Recommendation patterns: These verbs can introduce an activity in -ing form: They suggested taking a break.
Memory and interruption: Remember doing recalls an earlier action; stop doing means end an activity.
Preposition patterns: Here to is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Gerunds with Meaning Changes
matrix.summary: Choose gerund or infinitive patterns when the verb changes meaning according to the complement.

keyTakeaways: Memory versus duty: Remember doing recalls a past event; remember to do refers to a duty completed or not completed.
End versus interruption: Stop doing ends an activity; stop to do pauses one activity in order to do another.
Experiment and regret: Try doing tests a method; regret doing looks back, while regret to say introduces unwelcome news.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Complex Gerund Constructions
matrix.summary: Use possessive, passive, and perfect gerund constructions to package actions as precise nominal ideas.

keyTakeaways: Gerund subject: Use a possessive subject for a formal focus on the fact of someone’s action.
Passive gerund: Use a passive gerund when the subject of the gerund receives the action.
Perfect gerund: Use a perfect gerund to place the gerund action before the main verb or evaluation.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: To-Infinitives after Want, Need, and Plan
matrix.summary: The to-infinitive connects a person to an intended action or purpose.

keyTakeaways: Want and need to: to + base verb completes the meaning.
Plan to: plan to introduces an intended action.
Purpose to: to can answer why someone does something.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Infinitives for Purpose
matrix.summary: Use to + base verb to explain why an action happens.

keyTakeaways: Purpose with to: Use to + base verb when the second action explains why the first happens.
Purpose first: A purpose phrase can lead the sentence and take a comma.
Explicit purpose: In order to makes the purpose link especially clear in careful writing.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Verb Patterns with Infinitives
matrix.summary: Use infinitive patterns after verbs of decision, permission, refusal, and intention.

keyTakeaways: Verb plus infinitive: These verbs introduce an intended, attempted, or refused action with to + base verb.
Object plus infinitive: Use an object before the infinitive when one person gives another permission or encouragement.
Bare infinitive after make/let: Make and let do not take to before the base verb in this pattern.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Perfect and Passive Infinitives
matrix.summary: Use perfect and passive infinitives to express earlier actions, expected results, and affected subjects.

keyTakeaways: Perfect infinitive: Use to have done when the infinitive action happened before the main viewpoint.
Passive infinitive: Use to be done when the subject receives the action.
Perfect passive infinitive: Use to have been done for an earlier action received by the subject.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Nuanced Infinitive Structures
matrix.summary: Use advanced infinitive patterns to express evaluation, purpose, agency, and hypothetical or completed actions.

keyTakeaways: Explicit infinitive subject: Use for + object when the infinitive has a different understood subject.
Time and voice: Combine perfect and passive forms when the infinitive action is earlier or received.
Evaluation and consequence: Use infinitive clauses to express degree, consequence, or an unexpected result.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic -ed and -ing Adjectives
matrix.summary: Participial adjectives show either the source of a feeling or the person who experiences it.

keyTakeaways: -ing creates the feeling: an -ing adjective describes a thing or event.
-ed receives the feeling: an -ed adjective describes a person or animal affected by a feeling.
Participles as descriptions: some participles describe a state or result.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Boring, Bored, and Participial Adjectives
matrix.summary: Choose -ing for a source of a feeling and -ed for the experience.

keyTakeaways: Cause of a feeling: An -ing adjective describes something that causes a reaction.
Experienced feeling: An -ed adjective describes how someone feels.
Viewpoint contrast: Choose the ending from whether you mean the source or the experience.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Basic Participle Phrases
matrix.summary: Use present and perfect participle phrases to add background information without repeating a full clause.

keyTakeaways: Simultaneous action: An -ing phrase can show an action happening at the same time as the main clause.
Earlier action: Having finished shows that one action happened before the main clause.
Logical subject: The person or thing doing the participle action must be the subject of the main clause.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Participle Clauses
matrix.summary: Compress time, reason, and condition clauses with present, past, and perfect participle clauses.

keyTakeaways: Simultaneous or causal: An -ing clause can replace a clause with while, because, or as when the subject is shared.
Earlier event: Having completed the earlier action, the subject then performs the main action.
Passive compression: A past participle phrase can reduce a passive relative or condition clause.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Compressed Sophisticated Structures
matrix.summary: Use participle clauses and absolute constructions to compress background, circumstance, and evaluation in formal prose.

keyTakeaways: Perfect passive compression: Use having been done for an earlier action received by the subject.
Absolute construction: An absolute phrase has its own noun subject and provides background circumstance.
Dense evaluation: Participle phrases can package evidence, condition, or interpretation efficiently.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Say and Tell Reporting
matrix.summary: Reporting verbs let a speaker pass on another person's message.

keyTakeaways: Say + message: say introduces the words or message.
Tell + person + message: tell normally names the listener.
Tell someone to: tell + person + to gives an instruction.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Simple Say and Tell Reporting
matrix.summary: Report short statements and requests with say and tell.

keyTakeaways: Say and a message: Use say to introduce the message itself; that can be omitted.
Tell and a listener: Tell normally needs the person who receives the information.
Reported requests: Use this pattern when reporting a simple instruction or request.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Reported Speech and Backshift
matrix.summary: Report statements, questions, and requests while shifting tense and reference when the reporting verb is in the past.

keyTakeaways: Tense backshift: Present becomes past, will becomes would, and can becomes could when the past reporting viewpoint requires it.
Reference changes: Change pronouns and time or place words to match the new speaker and context.
Reported questions and requests: Reported questions use statement order; requests use an object plus to-infinitive.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Reporting Verbs and Patterns
matrix.summary: Use reporting verbs with their characteristic complements to describe claims, evidence, advice, and disagreement.

keyTakeaways: Gerund reporting: Use an -ing complement for an action or fact that is admitted, denied, or mentioned.
Object and infinitive: Use an object before the infinitive when the report is directed to someone.
Recommendation patterns: Choose a pattern that keeps the recommendation and its level of directness clear.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Nuanced Reporting and Stance
matrix.summary: Use reporting verbs and patterns to distinguish evidence, concession, allegation, implication, and evaluation.

keyTakeaways: Stance verbs: These verbs present a position while signalling different degrees of distance or challenge.
Concession and denial: Choose the complement according to whether the focus is a proposition or an action.
Implication: Use these verbs when evidence points toward a conclusion without stating it directly.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Identifying Relative Clauses
matrix.summary: A relative clause adds identifying information after a noun.

keyTakeaways: Who for people: who connects a person to more information.
That or which for things: that and which can connect a thing to a description.
Where for places: where connects a place to its use or action.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Defining Relative Clauses
matrix.summary: Use who, that, and which to identify a person or thing.

keyTakeaways: People with who: Use who to add identifying information about a person.
Things with that or which: Use that or which for a thing in a defining clause.
Essential information: Do not separate an identifying relative clause with commas.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Defining and Non-Defining Relatives
matrix.summary: Choose defining or non-defining relative clauses according to whether the information identifies the noun or simply adds detail.

keyTakeaways: Defining clause: The clause identifies the noun and cannot be removed without changing the reference.
Non-defining clause: Commas show that the added information is not needed to identify the noun.
Relative choice: Use who for people and which for things; do not use that in a non-defining clause.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Reduced Relative Clauses
matrix.summary: Reduce defining relative clauses when the active or passive relationship is clear.

keyTakeaways: Active reduction: Reduce who/which + be + -ing when the noun performs the action.
Passive reduction: Reduce who/which + be + past participle when the noun receives the action.
Restrictive focus: Keep the reduced information directly after the noun so the reference remains clear.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Complex Embedded Relative Clauses
matrix.summary: Use whose, preposition relatives, and nested relative structures to maintain precision in formal reference.

keyTakeaways: Possessive relative: Whose can refer to a person, organisation, or thing that possesses or contains something.
Formal preposition relative: Formal writing can place the preposition before which or whom.
Abstract antecedent: Use relative phrases to connect an abstract noun to its explanation or method.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: And, But, Or, and So
matrix.summary: Conjunctions make short sentences work together as one message.

keyTakeaways: And adds: and joins similar words or ideas.
But contrasts: but joins ideas that do not match.
Or and so: or offers a choice; so gives a result.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Because and So: Reason and Result
matrix.summary: Connect everyday ideas by showing why something happens or what results.

keyTakeaways: Because gives a reason: Because answers why the first clause is true or happens.
So gives a result: So shows what happens because of the first clause.
Choose one direction: Choose the linker that matches the direction of the relationship.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Although, Even Though, and Unless
matrix.summary: Express concession and conditions with conjunctions that connect complete clauses.

keyTakeaways: Concession: These conjunctions show that the main result happens despite an opposing fact.
Negative condition: Unless means if not and introduces the condition that prevents or changes a result.
Clause position: A leading concession or condition clause is followed by a comma.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Whereas, Despite, and Provided That
matrix.summary: Link formal comparisons, concession, and conditions with precise clause and preposition patterns.

keyTakeaways: Formal contrast: Whereas places two situations or viewpoints in contrast.
Concession phrase: Despite is followed by a noun phrase or -ing form, not a finite clause alone.
Condition for agreement: Provided that means if and only if the stated condition is satisfied.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Sophisticated Discourse Linking
matrix.summary: Use high-level linkers to organise concession, qualification, cause, and logical consequence across a sustained argument.

keyTakeaways: Concessive transition: These adverbials acknowledge a contrast with the previous proposition while continuing the argument.
Qualified scope: These linkers limit a claim or identify the premise on which it depends.
Formal concession: Notwithstanding introduces a concession in formal register and is not followed directly by a finite clause.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Prepositions of Place and Time
matrix.summary: Prepositions make relationships between a noun and place, time, or movement visible.

keyTakeaways: Place relationships: in, on, under, and next to describe position.
At, on, and in for time: at names a clock time, on a day, and in a month or year.
Preposition plus noun: a preposition is followed by a noun phrase.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: Prepositions of Movement
matrix.summary: Show destinations, entry, routes, and movement across surfaces.

keyTakeaways: Destination and origin: Use to for where movement ends and from for where it starts.
Inside and surface: Into ends inside a space; onto ends on a surface.
Routes: Through describes a route inside and out; across describes movement from one side to another.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Dependent Prepositions
matrix.summary: Use common adjective, verb, and noun combinations with their dependent prepositions.

keyTakeaways: Adjective patterns: Many adjectives select a particular preposition before a noun or gerund.
Verb patterns: The preposition is part of the verb pattern and should be learned with it.
Noun patterns: Nouns also form stable combinations with particular prepositions.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Complex and Idiomatic Preposition Phrases
matrix.summary: Use formal preposition phrases to frame topics, responsibility, method, risk, and representation.

keyTakeaways: Topic framing: These phrases specify the aspect or topic being discussed.
Method and risk: Use these phrases to describe how something happens or what danger accompanies it.
Representation and compliance: These phrases express acting for someone or following a rule or plan.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Subtle Idiomatic Preposition Selection
matrix.summary: Use formal prepositional phrases to express grounds, alignment, purpose, consequence, and institutional stance.

keyTakeaways: Grounds and evidence: These phrases specify the basis for a decision or reinterpretation.
Alignment and conflict: Use these phrases to compare a position with a principle, result, or policy.
Purpose and consequence: These phrases express intended purpose or a cost paid for an outcome.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.

matrix.title: Basic Comparatives and Superlatives
matrix.summary: Comparison helps a learner describe difference, equality, and extremes.

keyTakeaways: Comparative -er: short adjectives often take -er for two-way comparison.
More for longer adjectives: more comes before many longer adjectives.
Superlative: -est or most identifies the highest degree.
reviewPrompts: Write one new example from your own daily life.
Explain which meaning makes you choose this form.

matrix.title: More, Less, and As ... As
matrix.summary: Compare qualities and amounts with more, less, and as ... as.

keyTakeaways: More and less: Use more or less to compare a quality or amount with another one.
Equal comparison: Use as ... as when two things have the same degree of a quality.
Second comparison: Than introduces the comparison point.
reviewPrompts: Write one example from your own day.
Explain why another form would change the meaning.

matrix.title: Comparative Structures and Modifiers
matrix.summary: Make precise comparisons with modifiers, repeated comparatives, and the more ... the more patterns.

keyTakeaways: Comparative modifiers: Modifiers show how large the difference is: far more useful, slightly cheaper.
Linked change: This pattern describes two changes that develop together.
Quantity comparison: Choose fewer for countable items and less for uncountable amounts.
reviewPrompts: Write a new example from work, study, or daily life.
Explain the register or meaning choice in your example.

matrix.title: Complex Comparison and Degree
matrix.summary: Build comparisons that express scale, proportion, and evaluation with precise modifiers and structures.

keyTakeaways: Degree modifiers: These modifiers show the size of a difference in formal and analytical comparisons.
Proportional comparison: Use paired comparatives to show that one change affects another.
Framed comparison: These structures set a reference point or emphasise an unexpectedly high or equal degree.
reviewPrompts: Write a formal or workplace example using this structure.
Explain the change in meaning, time, or register created by the form.

matrix.title: Rhetorical and Nuanced Comparison
matrix.summary: Use comparison to evaluate degree, proportionality, approximation, and rhetorical contrast in sophisticated argument.

keyTakeaways: Calibrated degree: Use modifiers and stance adverbs to make an evaluation proportionate and defensible.
Proportional relation: Use paired comparatives to express a systematic relationship between changes.
Rhetorical quantity: These forms can minimise, emphasise, or question an apparent comparison.
reviewPrompts: Write a nuanced formal or spoken example using this structure.
Explain how the structure affects emphasis, certainty, or register.
